## Abstract {.unnumbered}

We build a neural-operator layer whose temporal kernel, for every spatial Fourier mode k, is a sum of poles and
residues that are polynomials in k. A trained layer can therefore be read as a dispersion relation λ(k). The time
axis is a first-order-hold exponential-integrator recursion: exact for piecewise-linear inputs, causal, and
independent of the window length.

**Linear systems.** In 1D diffusion, advection–diffusion–reaction, an undamped Euler–Bernoulli beam, and 2D
diffusion and anisotropic ADR, the layer recovers the dispersion relation at the data's oracle floor in every
seed. It does so either through a two-stage identification or through a joint fit from random starts. Three
details decide success:

- scaling the polynomials in $k/k_{\mathrm{ref}}$, with a second-order optimizer;
- excluding modes that the window or the sampling cannot resolve;
- a leaky cap on Re μ, because a hard cap traps starts.

**Nonlinear systems.** A deep version (lifting, channel-mixing pole layers, pointwise nonlinearities) is tested on
forced viscous Burgers and forced Cahn–Hilliard.

- It trains only with a separate, larger learning rate for its poles.
- At a matched budget it beats a band-covering Tucker FNO by 2× with 50 training samples, by 9 % with 400, and
  by 7× in time extrapolation.
- A small-amplitude linear probe recovers ν to 1–3 %, and the unstable band of Cahn–Hilliard ($k_c$ to 1 %).
- The FNO baselines are right inside the forced band but produce arbitrary poles outside it.
- **Limit:** a deep stack whose layer poles are all stable reproduces the growing modes in the probe over the
  training window. An unstable pole is therefore claimed only when probe and layer structure agree.
- **The form is what pays.** The same operator with a free pole per mode index (the per-mode generators of
  state-space and spectral-generator operators) matches the in-band accuracy and the time extrapolation, but its
  error on unseen forcing modes is 188× its test error, against 1.3× with poles in k.
- On PDEBench 1D Burgers the Tucker FNO is 1.8× more accurate at an equal real-parameter budget; the WPO's probe
  recovers ν within 3 % in one seed of three.

**Cahn–Hilliard application.**

- In the linear (spinodal) regime the layer recovers $k_c(\phi_0)$ from early-time data. With the mobility and
  gradient energy as inputs, it extrapolates beyond the training grid only with the physical form of the law.
- In 2D coarsening every stable model reproduces $L(t) \sim t^n$, and the Tucker FNO is 2× better pointwise. A WPO
  that diverged in rollout needed amplitude-scaled training starts, not a pole constraint.
- Trained on one box, the pole operator runs on a box twice as large with an unchanged error and the right
  coarsening law, without data or retraining. The FNO's mode-indexed weights do not transfer (35× the error).

## Introduction

Laplace-type neural operators [@cao2024lno; @ha2026lfno] represent the transient response with learned poles,
which invites a physical reading of those poles. The companion audit (project C) found that this reading fails by
default: poles do not move under published protocols, and fits are equally good with wrong poles. Project A asks
the constructive question. If the pole structure is made explicit in the wavenumber, can a model identify the
system's dispersion relation, and does that structure pay off in accuracy, data efficiency or extrapolation
against Fourier neural operators [@li2021fno]?

**Related work.** Several recent operators learn a stable linear generator per spatial Fourier mode:
structured state-space models keep diagonal poles per channel [@gu2022s4; @gu2022s4d] and serve as neural
operators for dynamical systems [@hu2025ssmno]; SGNO [@li2026sgno] learns a multiplier per Fourier index with an
exponential-integrator update; LGN-KM [@jamil2026lgn] ties a latent Koopman generator's damping to |k|^p and reads
dispersion branches from it, for unforced flows. "Poles per Fourier mode" is therefore not what is new here. The
claim of this paper is narrower: the poles are smooth functions μₙ(k) of the *physical* wavenumber in an
input-driven operator with an exact time axis, which is what makes them identifiable, continuable outside the
excited band and transferable across domain sizes. @sec-form tests that claim against free per-index poles in the
same architecture.

**Parameter budgets.** All budgets are counted in real degrees of freedom. The FNO-type baselines up to a35 were
matched by `numel`, which counts a complex weight once; their real budgets were about 1.9× the WPO's. This only
strengthens the comparisons the WPO wins; where the TFNO wins (2D coarsening, @sec-coarsening), it did so with
more parameters. a36 checks the effect on forced Burgers: a TFNO at the WPO's real budget is as accurate as the
larger one.

Every experiment below was pre-registered: predictions were committed before the runs, and every failed
prediction is reported.

## The wavenumber pole layer {#sec-layer}

For a linear PDE u_t = L u + f with periodic space, every Fourier mode obeys $d\hat u_k/dt=\lambda(k)\,\hat u_k+\hat f_k$. The layer
models the temporal kernel of mode k as

$$K(k,s)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_n(k)}{s-\mu_n(k)},\qquad
\mu_n(k)=\sum_j a_{nj}\,(k/k_{\mathrm{ref}})^{2j}+i\sum_j c_{nj}\,(k/k_{\mathrm{ref}})^{p_j},$$

with $\beta_n(k)$ a polynomial in k². The parameters are continuous in k, so the layer runs on any spatial grid.

- **Time axis.** The exact first-order-hold recursion $x_{j+1}=E\,x_j+b_0u_j+b_1u_{j+1}$, evaluated as a causal
  FFT convolution plus a first-sample correction. It is exact for inputs that are linear between samples, causal,
  and needs only Δt, so the same layer runs on a longer window or a finer Δt. This was the D1 decision; the Fourier
  time axis of LNO costs 4e-4 to 2e-3 on non-periodic inputs.
- **Options.**
  - `modes`: truncation to the forced band.
  - `re_max`: a smooth cap on Re μ. With `re_leak`, it keeps a slope above the cap (@sec-trap).
  - `stable`: Re μ = −softplus.
  - Any powers of k in Im μ: the beam's frequency c k² is even.
- **2D.** Re μ is a polynomial in |k|², and Im μ = c · k plus optional $|k|^p$. A real field needs
  μ(−k) = conj μ(k). The rfft2 layout holds negative $k_x$ only on the row $k_y = 0$, so the even imaginary terms get a
  half-plane sign there; tests caught the error before this was added.
- **Deep operator.** lift → [$K_l + W_l$, GELU] × L → projection. $K_l$ mixes channels, with N poles shared by all
  channel pairs and a residue matrix per pole. Summing the poles into one frequency-domain kernel per channel pair
  makes training 2.5× faster, with identical outputs.

## Linear systems {#sec-linear}

**Data.** Periodic x, 64 points, T = 5, n_t = 201. Each sample is forced at a few random modes with step, ramp,
PRBS or smooth time profiles. The truth is computed on a 32× finer time grid, so data and layer share no hold. The
oracle floor (the true λ in the layer) is 0.8–1.2 % and is set by jumps that fall between samples.

![Stage-1 per-mode poles against the truth (data seed 0). Filled: modes kept by the two cuts; hollow: modes cut
(too fast for Δt, or too slow for the window). Right: the beam's two poles per k; the cut modes k = 1–3 are where
the first beam recipe failed.](fig_linear.png){#fig-linear width=100%}

### A joint fit with Adam fails; the problem is optimization, not representation

The first validation fitted the polynomial jointly with Adam (a1).

- On diffusion, 3 of 5 seeds recover D to 0.02 % at the oracle floor. The other seeds, and every ADR seed, end in
  wrong basins with spurious k³, k⁴ terms.
- With k up to 16, one Adam step on a k⁴ coefficient moves Re μ by up to 6.5e4 × lr.

### A two-stage recipe recovers every system (a2–a6)

1. **Stage 1:** one pole per excited k (grid search, then Nelder–Mead; the residue by least squares).
2. **Stage 2:** weighted least squares for the polynomial.
3. **Fine-tune:** L-BFGS on the layer, with coefficients in $k/k_{\mathrm{ref}}$ units.

Two cuts, computed from the stage-1 estimates alone, decide which modes enter stage 2 (@fig-linear):

- a **resolution cut**, $|\hat\mu|\,\Delta t \le 0.25$ (fast modes are biased by the sampling);
- an **observability cut**, $\max(|\mathrm{Re}\,\hat\mu|, |\mathrm{Im}\,\hat\mu|)\,T \ge 2$. Slower modes fit as well with wrong poles; on the beam
  they wrecked 2 of 5 seeds before the cut was added.

With both cuts, every run in every system reaches the oracle floor:

| system (5 seeds each) | test / oracle | recovered constants |
|---|---|---|
| 1D diffusion, ADR | 0.98–1.10 | D, v, k_r within 0.05 % |
| beam (N = 2, poles ±i c k²) | 1.00–1.02 | c within 0.35 %, Re/Im ≤ 2.3e-4 |
| 2D diffusion, anisotropic ADR | 1.000–1.002 | D, v = (0.4, −0.3) within 0.03 % |

: Linear validations with the two-stage recipe and both cuts. {#tbl-linear}

### Stage 1 is not needed; a hard cap traps starts {#sec-trap}

A joint fit from 8–16 random starts, with the same $k_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and L-BFGS and selection by validation error, also
reaches the oracle in all 25 data seeds (a7).

- The failing starts were the same indices in every data seed. They ended with Re μ at the cap for all k, where
  the soft minimum has no gradient.
- A leak of 0.05 above the cap fixes it (a8): every start succeeds for diffusion and ADR, and 9–15 of 16 for the
  beam.
- Stage 1 remains useful as a model-free diagnostic and as a deterministic start.

## Deep operators on nonlinear systems {#sec-deep}

**Forced viscous Burgers** (ν = 0.1, 64 points, T = 5). The forcing scale is log-uniform over [0.03, 1], so up to
91 % of a sample is not the linear response. Linearized at u = 0, λ(k) = −ν k².

**Probe.** Single-mode inputs at small amplitude; the odd part of the response; the stage-1 identification per
mode; both cuts.

### The poles need their own learning rate

At a shared Adam learning rate (1e-3), the poles stayed at their initialization (a9). Re μ was flat in k, some
poles had Re μ > 0, and errors over (5, 10] blew up to 3–8. The k² coefficient of −ν k² is −25.6 in k / k_ref
units, beyond reach in 4000 steps. A pole learning rate 30× larger cut the error 2.4–3.4× (a10), as (C) found for
LNO.

### Accuracy, extrapolation and data efficiency

The first FNO baseline (n_modes 12 × 12) kept only |k| ≤ 6 and 7 temporal frequencies: below the forced band. We
found this after the run and replaced it with band-covering baselines (a13). Both models then got the same
learning-rate sweep.

| model | params | test (N = 200) | error over (5, 10] | probe residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO (stable) | 59.5 k | **0.024** | **0.04** | **0.003** |
| TFNO (Tucker, n_modes 32 × 64) | 110.6 k real (59.1 k numel) | 0.031 | 0.29 | 0.008–0.25 |
| TFNO, real budget (a36) | 54.6 k | 0.028 | 0.29 | – |
| FNO (full rank, 18×) | 1.08 M | 0.042 (overfits) | 0.29 | 0.36–0.49 |

: Forced Burgers, 3 seeds; time extrapolation from training on T = 5 to T = 10. {#tbl-burgers}

![Forced Burgers: test error against training-set size (mean and min–max over 3 seeds; nested training sets, same
test set).](fig_data_eff.png){#fig-data width=50%}

- **Data efficiency** (@fig-data, a14): the TFNO / WPO error ratio is 1.96 at N = 50, then 1.42, 1.28 and 1.09 at
  N = 400. The WPO's advantage is an inductive bias, and it shrinks as data grow.
- **Resolution** (a15): every model transfers to 32 and 128 points within 9 %. At Δt/2 the WPO's error drops by
  20 %, the FNOs' by 4–8 %.

### What the probe reads

![Per-mode probe poles. Left, Burgers: inside the forced band (shaded) every model is right; above it only the WPO
continues −ν k². The FNO variants return arbitrary poles. Beyond the resolution cut (dashed) the estimates are
biased for every model, the solver included. Right, Cahn–Hilliard: all three models, including the stable
control, reproduce the growing modes.](fig_probe.png){#fig-probe width=100%}

- **Burgers.** Every model's linearization is right to 1–2 % inside the forced band (@fig-probe). Outside it, only
  the WPO continues the dispersion relation (k = 9 within 1–4 %), and only its small-amplitude response is
  LTI-consistent (residual 0.003).
- **A bias that was not physics.** An earlier probe bias (ν̂ 11–14 % high, a10) was the polynomial summary
  absorbing over-damping at the weakly forced top of the band. It vanished with longer training (a11). A
  polynomial summary needs its residual reported.
- **Cahn–Hilliard** (M = 0.1, κ = 0.04; λ(k) = M k²(1 − κ k²), $k_c$ = 5). With Re μ > 0 allowed, the WPO's probe
  gives $k_c$ = 4.99–5.03 and every sign right (a16), against 5.107 from the solver's own probe. The TFNO's in-band
  poles are right in one seed, but out-of-band poles spoil its fit in all three.

### Is it the physical-wavenumber form? (a36) {#sec-form}

Same data, same architecture and training as the WPO, but each layer's poles are a free table over the 22
retained mode indices (residues stay polynomial): the per-mode generator of S4D- or SGNO-type operators. Two
extra tests: the probe's poles outside the forced band (k = 9–16), and a set forced only at k = 9–12, which no
training sample excites. The original LNO (v2, steady modes raised to cover the band) is added at the same real
budget.

| model | test | (5, 10] / test | probe outside the band (k = 9–16) | unseen modes / test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO, poles in k | **0.024** | **1.8** | **0.12** | **1.3** |
| WPO, poles per index | **0.023** | **1.7** | 0.99 | 188 |
| TFNO, real budget | 0.028 | 10.3 | 0.89 | 32 |
| LNO v2 | 0.38 | 1.2 | 1.06 | 2.9 |

: Forced Burgers, 3 seeds (means); probe column: mean relative pole error against −νk². {#tbl-form}

- Inside the forced band the form does not matter: same test error, same time extrapolation (the FOH recursion
  carries it), and every model's probe is right at k ≤ 8.
- Outside it only the polynomial poles continue. Per-index poles at modes the data never excite stay where they
  started, and an input there produces a response 4× the truth's size.
- The original LNO, at this budget, does not fit forced Burgers (16× the WPO's error). Five of six predictions
  held; the LNO's predicted extrapolation ratio above 2.5 failed because its in-window error is already large.

### A public benchmark: PDEBench 1D Burgers (a37)

Initial field → trajectory (ν = 0.01, 256 × 41, PDEBench's split and nRMSE). The repository solver reproduces the
benchmark to 3e-4 through an exact rescaling, so the linearization is known: λ_m = −0.1257 m².

- The Tucker FNO (equal real budget) is 1.8× more accurate (nRMSE 0.026 against 0.045); both are unchanged at 4×
  the resolution.
- The probe separates the models less than on forced Burgers: both get the slowest modes (m ≤ 4); at m = 8–10 two
  WPO seeds are within 10 % and no FNO seed is. The WPO's ν is 2.4 %, 9 % and 35 % off; the prediction of 5 % in
  every seed failed. Without forcing that isolates modes, the data constrain the small-amplitude response only
  partly.
- The pre-registered WPO runs ended in nan from an overflow in a masked branch of the time kernel for very fast
  poles; the reported runs repeat them unchanged after the fix (post hoc).

### An identifiability limit: growth emulated by stable layers

A stable control, with every layer pole at Re μ ≤ 0, fits Cahn–Hilliard as well as the WPO. Its probe reproduces
the growing modes to three digits. Its layer poles sit just below zero: a cascade of near-integrators produces
$t^n$ growth, indistinguishable from $e^{0.58t}$ on [0, 5]. A longer probe window does not separate the two either,
because the linearization leaves the linear regime (growth ×300 over T = 10).

Within a finite window, then, the probe of the whole operator does not identify an unstable pole. We claim one
only when probe and layer structure agree: Re μ > 0 allowed, used, and located in the band. This is the same rule
as (C)'s trust rule for poles.

### Spinodal decomposition across compositions (application 2, stage 1) {#sec-spinodal}

Around a uniform composition φ₀ the linearization is λ(k; φ₀) = Mk²(1 − 3φ₀²) − Mκk⁴, unstable for
k < k_c(φ₀) inside the spinodal |φ₀| < 1/√3. We trained the initial-condition path of project D alone,
û(k, t) = γ(k) û₀(k) e^{μ(k, φ₀)t}, with φ₀ read from the mean of the initial field and μ a law in k² and φ₀² (6 reals).
Training used early-time, unforced data at eight compositions (0 to 0.7); evaluation used five held-out ones.

| model | test / oracle, held-out φ₀ | φ̂_s (0.57735) | k̂_c(0), k̂_c(0.3), k̂_c(0.5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| law in k² and φ₀² | **0.995–1.006** | **0.57733–0.57736** | **5.0000, 4.2719, 2.500** |
| same, Re μ ≤ 0 (LNO constraint) | 130–1710 | 0.78 | 4.65, 4.31, 3.60 |
| no φ₀ dependence | 106–1118 | – | – |

: 1D Cahn–Hilliard, linear regime, 5 data seeds; the oracle floor is the nonlinear residual (≤ 3.6e-3). {#tbl-spinodal}

- The layer recovers the stability diagram of the linear regime: k_c(φ₀) to 1e-4 and the spinodal to 3e-5. It
  extrapolates to φ₀ = 0.8, beyond the training range and outside the spinodal.
- The model class contains the truth, so this shows identifiability from early-time data, not discovery of the form.
- The stability constraint is not a small bias. It distorts the stable modes as well and is off by up to 1700×.

**Mobility and gradient energy as inputs** (stage 3, linear regime). With M and κ varied on a 2 × 2 grid and fed to
the layer, the law in the form of the linearization, μ = M(ak² + bk²φ₀²) + Mκ·dk⁴ (3 reals), reaches the oracle
(≤ 1.01×) at M twice and κ half the grid's range, with k_c within 1.5e-4. A 16-term law that contains the truth but
not its form is 1–17× the oracle off the grid, depending on the seed; an MLP law is 10⁴× off even between grid
points. The response is e^{μt}, so in the unstable band an error in the law becomes exponential in the output.

## 2D deep operator {#sec-2d}

The 2D layer and operator carry the same structure: Re μ is isotropic in |k|², with an advection vector and the
half-plane sign. On forced 2D Cahn–Hilliard (32², $k_c$ = 5) we compare WPO-2D (18.7 k parameters) with a 3D
Tucker FNO (15.0 k, the closest rank) over 3 seeds and 6000 steps (a17).

| model | params | test | probe $k_c$ (solver 5.003) | median in-band per-mode error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO-2D | 18.7 k | **0.030–0.036** | **4.98–5.09** | **0.2–0.6 %** |
| TFNO, tuned (a18) | 20.4 k | 0.071–0.089 | 3.76–5.06 | 3.9–8.3 % |
| TFNO, untuned (a17) | 15.0 k | 0.100–0.125 | 4.49–4.96 | 3–16 % |

: Forced 2D Cahn–Hilliard, 3 seeds. {#tbl-ch2d}

- The probe of WPO-2D is right mode by mode, along both (k, 0) and (k, k), so the learned dispersion relation is
  isotropic as the truth is.
- A budget-matched TFNO with a learning-rate sweep (a18) closes about a third of the gap. The WPO-2D keeps a 2.6×
  lower test error and a per-mode linearization an order of magnitude more accurate.
- One pre-registered prediction failed: that the untuned TFNO's $k_c$ would miss by more than 10 % in most seeds.
  2 of 3 seeds landed within 10 %.

### Rollout into coarsening (application 2, stage 2) {#sec-coarsening}

Unforced 2D Cahn–Hilliard after a critical quench (128² truth, 64² models): from the true state at t = 1, 20
chained windows of one time unit, in which L(t) grows from 1.5 to 3.5 (exponent 0.271 on this range; 0.261 on a
4π box, so the 2π box is not size-limited).

| setting | model | one window | window 20 | L(21) / truth | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2π (a31) | WPO-2D | 0.033–0.035 | 0.67–0.74 | 0.975–0.991 | 0.261–0.268 |
| | TFNO | **0.015–0.022** | **0.34–0.39** | 0.967–0.974 | 0.255–0.257 |
| | FNO-2D (AR) | 0.035–0.043 | 0.81–0.91 | 0.968–1.015 | 0.247–0.267 |
| 2π, scaled starts (a33) | WPO-2D | 0.035–0.039 | 0.70–0.89 | 0.961–0.990 | 0.244–0.262 |
| | TFNO | **0.018–0.020** | **0.39–0.43** | 0.974–0.976 | 0.255–0.257 |
| 4π, trained on 2π (a34) | WPO-2D | **0.035–0.041** | **0.85** | 1.04–1.08 | 0.272–0.286 |
| | TFNO | 0.66–0.71 | 1.41 | 2.15–2.19 | 0.31–0.35 |
| 4π, trained on 4π (a35) | TFNO | 0.031–0.038 | 0.83 | 1.03–1.04 | 0.270–0.274 |
| | TFNO, modes × 2 | **0.019–0.023** | **0.63** | 1.02–1.03 | 0.265–0.273 |

: 2D coarsening, 3 seeds per row (ranges; window 20 is the mean when one number is given). In a31 one WPO-2D seed
diverged; its row shows the two stable seeds. No other run diverged. The 2π truth has n = 0.271 and the 4π truth
n = 0.261. {#tbl-coarsening}

- **The statistics are a weak test.** Every stable run reproduces the coarsening law (L within 8 %, n within
  0.03). A field frozen at t = 1 gives L(21) / truth = 0.43. Per-window errors separate the models more.
- **On the training box the TFNO is the better surrogate**, 2× more accurate per window and in rollout, with or
  without scaled starts.
- **The WPO-2D divergence is a gap in data coverage, not a pole problem.**
  - In a31 one WPO-2D seed diverges, with its poles at the growth cap. Changing the cap does not help: with
    stable poles, a cap of 0.3, or a cap of 1 without the leak, 2, 3 and 2 of 3 seeds diverge (a32).
  - The window map lacks a restoring force (a32b, post hoc). Scale a true state by a = 2, and the truth returns
    max |u| at 0.50 × the scaled maximum. The TFNO returns 0.76; every WPO-2D run returns 1.5–4.8, stable poles
    included. An overshoot past ±1 then persists.
  - The training starts never leave |u| < 1.05. One amplitude-scaled copy per training window
    (a ~ U[0.7, 1.6], target from the solver) gives a gain of 0.58–0.66 at a = 2 and no divergence in any seed
    (a33). Pointwise rollout does not improve.
- **The pole operator transfers across box sizes; the TFNO does not.**
  - A WPO-2D trained on 2π runs on a 4π box at the same spacing with no data and no retraining: each layer gets
    the new length and twice the mode count. The poles are functions of the physical wavenumber, so the
    one-window error is unchanged (1.02–1.03×) and the 4π rollouts keep the law (a34).
  - The TFNO's spectral weights belong to mode indices, which on 4π are other physical wavenumbers: 35× the
    error, domains growing 2.2× too fast (@fig-transfer).
  - A TFNO trained on 4π with its mode count doubled is 1.8× more accurate than the transferred WPO-2D (a35). With
    the original mode count it is at 0.034, close to the WPO-2D's 0.038, which never saw the 4π box.

![Rollout on the 4π box from the true state at t = 1. Left: length scale L(t); the WPO-2D trained on 2π follows the
truth, the TFNO trained on 2π coarsens 2.2× too fast. Right: per-window rollout error; the TFNO trained on the 4π
box itself is the accuracy reference (a34, a35).](fig_transfer.png){#fig-transfer width=100%}

## Polynomial or MLP pole functions (RQ4) {#sec-rq4}

The plan offers an MLP μ(k) as the flexible alternative. To compare the two, we train only on data forced at k ≤ 8
and test at k = 9–16 (a19; diffusion, ADR, beam; 5 seeds; same joint fit).

- In band, both reach the oracle (MLP ≤ 1.05×).
- Out of band, the polynomial stays at 1.00–1.08× the oracle with a dispersion error ≤ 0.5 %. The MLP is at 4.6–44×
  with 13–55 %.

When the form is right, the polynomial wins on both accuracy and interpretability.

With a dispersion relation that is not polynomial, fractional diffusion λ = −0.15|k|^1.5 (a22), the order reverses:

- Trained on k ≤ 16, the MLP is at 1.02–1.04× the oracle and the polynomial at 5.4–8.5×.
- Out of band, neither extrapolates. The wrong polynomial is catastrophic there (3500×, driven by its k⁴ term); the
  MLP degrades to 12–18×.

This gives a practical check: fit both. If the polynomial matches the MLP in band, its form is supported and its
extrapolation can be trusted. If not, use the MLP and do not extrapolate.

## Delay: a first process-dynamics step {#sec-delay}

Delay is not rational, so pole-only kernels must approximate it. A pole–residue–delay layer, K(s) = Σ β e^{−θs}/(s − μ),
with an exact delayed first-order hold, is evaluated on FOPDT and SOPDT data whose delays are not multiples of the
sample time (a20).

- **FOPDT:** θ, K and τ recovered to 1e-4.
- **SOPDT:** θ within 1.1 %, K and τ within 0.08 %.
- **Pole-only layer (4 complex poles):** fits to 1.06–1.95× the oracle, but has no delay to read.
- **ARX:** resolves θ only to the sample.
- **Under 5 % output noise (a21):** the delay layer, fitted by output error, keeps FOPDT exact to 0.2 % and SOPDT's
  θ within 3.3 %. Equation-error ARX is biased by the noise, with τ off by 52–86 %.

### Delay against dispersion, and a nonlinear CSTR

- **Dispersion reactor** (a24). Sensors at distances L = 1–3 downstream of a source.
  - Lumped FOPDT / SOPDT fits give a dead time θ below L/v, growing faster than L, and leave 5–17 % of the signal
    unexplained.
  - The wavenumber layer on the field reads v = 0.50001, D = 0.01999, k_r = 0.10000.
  - Transport inside the domain is the −ivk of λ(k), not a dead time.
- **Delay and dispersion together** (a25). ADR with an input delay of 0.73. The wavenumber layer with one shared delay
  recovers θ and λ(k) within 0.04 %. Without it, the error is 14–44× the oracle.
- **CSTR** (a23). Exothermic CSTR at its upper steady state, Jacobian pair −0.769 ± 0.960i.
  - The time-only WPO's probe is within 0.1–0.6 % of the pair, at 2.2× lower test error than an FNO of the same
    size.
  - The FNO's probe and the best linear fit are also within 1 %. At a stable focus, every reading of the
    linearization agrees.
- **Closed loop with measurement noise** (a26, a28).
  - With a PI loop and 2 % noise, the output-error fits (WPO probe, linear pair) stay within 1.1 % of the Jacobian
    pair.
  - Equation-error ARX fails in every regime. An amplitude gate reduces its error from 88 % to 7 % noise-free, but
    the noise then destroys it.
- **Open boundaries** (a27). A Danckwerts reactor, inlet → outlet, Péclet 20.
  - A delay plus two lags fits best: mean delay 0.97 against a residence time of 1.0.
  - Modal or free poles do not recover the eigenvalues: they spend themselves approximating the transport delay.
  - The pole readout is physical for translation-invariant problems; open-boundary convective systems need the
    boundary handling of project (D).

## Discussion

- **What is identifiable.**
  - In linear problems, the full dispersion relation, from data alone, given scaled parameters and modes that the
    window and the sampling resolve.
  - In deep nonlinear models, the linearization at rest, through a probe, inside the forced band. That is true of
    FNO-type models as well.
  - What the pole structure adds: a dispersion relation that continues outside the forced band, and an
    LTI-consistent linear response. Free poles per mode index do not give this (@sec-form): the gain comes from
    the physical-wavenumber form, not from having poles.
- **Where the accuracy gain comes from.** Data efficiency (2× at 50 samples) and time extrapolation (7×). The
  in-window error at 400 samples is close to parity (9 %).
- **Where the structure pays, and where it does not.** It pays in four places:
  - identification: dispersion relations and the spinodal band, from data;
  - continuation outside the forced band;
  - extrapolation in physical parameters, when the law has the right form (@sec-spinodal);
  - transfer across domain sizes without retraining (@sec-coarsening).

  It does not pay in pointwise accuracy in the strongly nonlinear regime on the training domain. There the TFNO
  is 2× better (2D coarsening, with about 1.9× the real parameters; also project D's Cahn–Hilliard with initial
  fields) and 1.8× better on PDEBench Burgers at an equal real budget.
- **Rollout stability is a data question.** The WPO-2D coarsening divergence was cured by amplitude-scaled
  training starts, not by any pole constraint.
- **Training details decide the outcome**, as in (C):
  - scaling the polynomials;
  - a pole learning rate in deep models;
  - a leaky rather than hard cap on Re μ;
  - checking that a baseline's modes cover the band. We got this wrong once.

## Limitations {.unnumbered}

- Two 2D deep experiments: forced (@sec-2d, an untuned, slightly smaller baseline) and coarsening
  (@sec-coarsening). Domain transfer was tested for one factor (2π to 4π), one time range (to t = 21), and a
  WPO-2D trained on 2π only; a WPO-2D trained on 4π was not run.
- Two nonlinear systems, both with a known linearization at rest.
- One parameter budget (59 k); FNO-type baselines from neuraloperator with a learning-rate sweep but no
  architecture search. Up to a35 the baselines were matched by `numel` (about 1.9× the WPO's real parameters);
  only a36 and a37 match real budgets, and the 2D comparisons have not been rerun.
- One public benchmark (PDEBench 1D Burgers), unforced; the SSM and spectral-generator operators of the related
  work were represented by per-index poles inside the WPO, not run from their own code.
- The probe is a small-amplitude linearization at u = 0. Linearizations about other uniform states were learned
  only in the linear regime of one system (@sec-spinodal), not probed from a deep model. Extrapolation in M and κ
  was shown for a law with the right form; no form was discovered.
- The oracle floor of the data (steps and PRBS between samples) limits every test error to about 1 %.
